exp.0:10:
This verse tells Gaius: do not imitate what is wrong; follow what is good. "Beloved" is an affectionate way of addressing him. The verse's own wording, "Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good," is the same message. Whoever does good shows that they belong to God; whoever does evil has not seen God, meaning they do not truly know him.

The elder John is speaking, in a personal letter to his friend Gaius. He tells him that Diotrephes, who wanted to be first, was speaking badly about them and was not welcoming the brothers who traveled teaching. For this reason John warns Gaius not to copy that bad example. He then mentions Demetrius as someone worthy of imitation.

Today, before following someone's example, look at how they treat others. Imitate those who serve with humility and welcome others, and avoid pride, gossip and harshness, even when they come from people in authority.
exp.0:8:
The explanation says that the author wrote a letter to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, will not accept the author's instruction. The phrase about being first is kept in plain form, matching the verse, and the refusal is described in the verse's own terms, as not accepting instruction.

The one who writes is the elder, as he introduces himself at the beginning of the letter, and he writes to Gaius. The traveling missionary brothers who went out preaching needed lodging and support. Diotrephes rejected them, spoke badly of the author, and even expelled those who wanted to help them. We do not know exactly what his office was, but his attitude is clear.

For today: examine your heart. Serve in your church without seeking to be first, and welcome kindly others who work for the gospel.
exp.0:6:
It says that some brothers went out to preach and to serve for the sake of the Name, which refers to Christ, and that they did not accept anything from the Gentiles, that is, from those outside the faith.

The one speaking is John, called "the elder," who writes to his dear friend Gaius. The traveling brothers were missionaries who had been well received by Gaius. John explains that they did not accept anything from unbelievers, so that no one could think they were preaching for money. That is why believers should support them.

For today: give generously to those who serve God sincerely, whether through prayer, offerings, or hospitality. In this way you take part in their work and help the gospel move forward.
exp.0:1:
John tells his dear friend Gaius that he hopes everything will go well for him in every way, and that he will enjoy good health, just as his soul is already doing well. "Prosper" means that things go well for him, and "in every way" means in all areas of life. The soul's prospering refers to his spiritual life, which is healthy and strong.

The one speaking is "the elder," whom many understand to be the apostle John, although the letter does not give his name. He writes to Gaius, a believer known for his faithfulness and for welcoming the brothers who traveled. This greeting was common in letters of the time, and here John joins it with a sincere wish of affection. It is not a promise of wealth, but a prayer for his well-being.

Today we can pray for the people we love, asking for health and well-being for them, but caring first for their spiritual life. May our inner peace grow more than anything else.
exp.0:13:
He says that the author hopes to visit Gaius soon and talk with him face to face, that is, in person. He wishes him peace, a greeting that means well-being and harmony. He sends greetings from the friends who are with him and asks Gaius to greet each of their friends there by name.

The one speaking is the elder, as he introduces himself at the beginning of the letter, and he writes to his dear Gaius. He does not say everything in writing, because he prefers to speak in person. Little is discussed about who this elder is; Christian tradition has identified him with John, although the letter does not give his name.

Today we can imitate this personal care. Some things are better said in person. Also, greeting others by name shows them that they are valued. This week, visit or call someone and acknowledge them by name.
exp.0:2:
The writer was overjoyed when some fellow believers arrived and reported on Gaius's devotion to the truth. The explanation notes that the wording behind "overjoyed" is about being glad, and that the phrase "testified about your devotion to the truth" means they spoke well of how Gaius holds to the faith. Continuing to walk in the truth means living steadily according to what he believes.

The one speaking is identified as the elder, traditionally understood to be the apostle John, although the letter does not give his name. He writes to Gaius, whom he loves as a friend and as a child in the faith. Some traveling believers came back with good news about Gaius's life, and this encouraged John greatly.

For today: our faith shows in the way we live, not only in what we say. Strive for your way of treating others, your honesty, and your service to give a good witness of Christ. Also be ready to rejoice and to encourage others when you see them doing well in their faith.
exp.0:9:
He says that John, if he comes to visit them, will call attention to what Diotrephes is doing. This man is spreading malicious slander against John and his companions. Not satisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers, forbids others who want to welcome them, and even puts those who do out of the church.

The one speaking is John, who in this letter calls himself "the elder," and he writes to his friend Gaius. There were missionaries who traveled preaching and needed a place to stay. Diotrephes, who wanted to be first, turned them away. John wants Gaius to keep supporting them. We do not know in detail what teaching or conflict lay behind this.

For today: examine whether the desire to have first place leads you to shut the door on others. Practice hospitality, and give generously to those who serve with humility.
exp.0:7:
Believers ought to support those who go out to share the gospel. Here, supporting them includes offering them a place to stay and help for the journey. "Such" refers to those traveling brothers, and being fellow workers for the truth means working alongside them in God's work.

The elder John writes to his beloved friend Gaius. Some missionaries sent by John had traveled out of love for Christ, asking nothing from unbelievers. Gaius had welcomed them well, while Diotrephes, out of pride, rejected them. John encourages Gaius to keep supporting them.

Today we can support missionaries, pastors, or brothers and sisters who serve, through prayer, offerings, lodging, or a word of encouragement. In this way we share in their work, even if we ourselves do not go out to preach.
exp.0:12:
He says he has many more things to tell his friend, but he would rather not write them down with pen and ink, that is, in a letter. The following verses explain why: he hopes to visit soon and speak with him face to face.

The one speaking is "the elder," as he introduces himself at the start of this letter. Tradition identifies him with John the apostle, although the letter does not give his name. He is writing to Gaius, a dear brother who welcomes believers who are traveling. After praising Gaius and warning him about Diotrephes, the author closes warmly and saves the other matters for a conversation in person.

Some things are better said face to face than in writing. Today, instead of settling everything through messages, we can make a visit or a phone call to encourage someone, clear up a misunderstanding, or share what we feel from the heart.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that some traveling brothers spoke before the church about the love Gaius showed them. John asks him to keep sending them on their way in a manner worthy of God, and he assures him that by doing so he will do well.

John, now an elderly man, writes to his beloved friend Gaius. He rejoices because Gaius walks in the truth and has welcomed with hospitality brothers who went out to preach the gospel. They did not accept help from unbelievers, so they depended on the generosity of other Christians. John wants Gaius to continue supporting them.

For today: think of someone who serves God, such as a missionary, a pastor, or a teacher, and help them in a concrete way. You can pray for them, give an offering, host them, or encourage them with a message.
exp.0:0:
The writer introduces himself simply as "the elder" and greets Gaius with warmth, calling him "beloved." He says he loves him "in the truth," meaning with a sincere love, not with empty words or mere politeness. In this verse, "whom I love" points to the person being loved, Gaius.

The writer names himself only as "the elder." Tradition identifies him with the apostle John, although the letter does not state his name. Gaius was a believer known for his hospitality toward the brothers who traveled. John writes to encourage him and to clarify who truly walks in the truth.

Today we can imitate this greeting. Think of a brother or sister in your church and tell them today, sincerely, that you value them and that you pray for them. A simple and true message can strengthen another person a great deal.
exp.0:11:
Everyone speaks well of Demetrius, and even "the truth itself" backs him up, meaning that his life agrees with what the gospel teaches. John and those who are with him also give a good testimony. "You know" that John's testimony is true, and John reminds them that his word can be trusted.

The one speaking is John, the elder, and he writes to Gaius, a beloved brother. Diotrephes refused to receive the brothers who traveled teaching. For this reason John presents Demetrius, probably the one carrying the letter, so that they will receive him well. Some believe he was a messenger; the text does not say this with certainty.

For today: value and support people whose lives confirm what they say they believe. Also seek to have your own character speak well of Christ. Before following anyone, look at their conduct and at what other healthy believers say about them.
exp.0:3:
The explanation says that for the author there is no greater joy than to know that his children live according to the truth. The author's own words say he has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth, so the explanation here refers to news reaching him about them. "Walking" is the everyday way of describing how a person lives day by day. "The truth" refers to what God teaches and to living it out in practice.

The one speaking is the elder, as he presents himself in verse 1, and Christian tradition identifies him with John. He writes to Gayo, whom he loves. When he says "my children," he is speaking with affection of people he has guided in the faith, not necessarily of children by blood. Some traveling brothers told him that Gayo was living faithfully, and that gladdened him greatly.

For today: if you guide or accompany others in the faith, rejoice when they grow and live out what they believe. Encourage them with a word or a prayer, and seek to make your own life consistent with the truth you teach.
exp.0:4:
He says that Gaius, whom John calls "beloved," is faithful in what he does for the brothers, especially since they are strangers to him. "Faithful" means showing loyalty and steadiness. Here, "strangers" refers to believers from other places who came to visit, not necessarily people of another nationality.

The speaker is John, the elder, who writes a personal letter to Gaius. The traveling believers, probably missionaries sent out to preach, had been warmly welcomed by Gaius. John rejoices and encourages him to keep helping them. It is not known with certainty who this Gaius was, since several men had that name.

Today we can imitate Gaius: open the door, and give food, lodging, or help to those who serve God or are in need, even if we do not know them well. Small acts of hospitality, done faithfully, please God.

sum.0: The elder writes to his beloved Gaius to commend him for walking in the truth and for faithfully supporting the brothers who travel around preaching. He asks him to keep on helping them, and he warns that Diotrephes, who loves to be first, refuses to welcome the brothers and speaks evil of them. He encourages Gaius to keep following what is good, and he speaks highly of Demetrius.
